source_text:
ἵνα δὲ μὴ τὴν ἐντολὴν ἢ τὸν ταύτην δεδωκότα θεὸν αἰτιάσωνταί τινες, γείτονι καὶ ὁμοσπόρῳ ἐχρήσατο ῥήματι τοιάδε φάσκων· οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι ὁ νόμος ἅγιος καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ δικαία καὶ
ἀγαθή. Ἐπεὶ οὖν οὐδ' αὐτὴ ἡ ἁμαρτία, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ὁ διάβολος, φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ ἁμαρτία ἐστίν, ἐπιφέρει λέγων· ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερ 4 βολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς. τὸ γὰρ κατ' οὐσίαν τὶ ὂν τὸ πλέον καὶ τὸ ἔλαττον οὐκ ἐπιδέξεται· ἔστιν γὰρ ὅπερ ἐστίν, ἀεὶ τοῦτο ὂν ὅπερ ἐστὶν οὐσιωδῶς. τῷ γὰρ γινομένῳ καὶ ἐπιγινομένῳ τι, εἴτε ὀλίγον εἴτε καθ' ὑπερβολήν, ἕτερός ἐστι κατ' οὐσίαν τῶν αὐτῷ ἐπιγινομένων· τὸ γὰρ πόσον οὐκ οὐσία ἀλλὰ περὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἐστίν, οὐκ ὂν οὐσία. ἡ ἄρα τοίνυν καλουμένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀποστόλου ἁμαρτία τὸ πλέον ἐπιδεχομένη ἁμαρτήσειν, ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία. ἄρα καὶ τοῦ εἶναι ἁμαρτία, ᾗ ἁμαρτία ἐστίν, ἀρχὴν ἔλαβεν, οὐκ οὖσα καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἐν ἀρχῇ κατὰ τὸ ἡμαρτηκέναι ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία. διὸ δὴ καὶ τὴν ἐπίτασιν τοῦ γενέσθαι καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸν ἐσομένῳ χρόνῳ σημαίνει οὕτω λέγων· ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς. εἰ δὲ λέγοιεν· καὶ πῶς ἂν εἴη ἀγαθὴ καὶ δικαία; πῶς δὲ ἁγία ἡ ἐντολὴ καὶ ὁ νόμος, ὁπότε διὰ τῆς ἀφορμῆς αὐτῶν 2 ἁμαρτωλὸς καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἐγένετο ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία; πρὸς ταῦτα ἀκουέτωσαν ὅτι οὐκ, εἴ τι καταβλάπτεται, ἤδη καὶ ἡ ἀφορμὴ δι' ἣν βλάπτεται φαύλη ἐστὶ καὶ πονηρά· οὐδὲ γὰρ ὅτι οἱ ἀνόδως καὶ ἀμέτρως ἐνατενίζοντες τῷ ἡλίῳ βλάπτονται τὰς ὄψεις, ἤδη καὶ τὸν ἥλιόν φαμεν πονηρόν· οὐδ' ὅτι καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ὁ διάβολος ἁμαρτωλὸς γέγονε τῷ ἐπικεχειρηκέναι κατὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἤδη καὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ φαῦλον καὶ πονηρὸν εἶναι λέγομεν. Οἶδα δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἐμοί, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου, ἀγαθόν. νῦν εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον ἐξηγεῖται. καὶ ὅτι στερηθεὶς τὸν θεὸν ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτῷ, ἀντὶ τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς θάνατον καταλλαξάμενος–καὶ γὰρ θάνατος οὐχ ὁ κοινὸς μόνος τῶν μελῶν αὐτοῦ ἐκράτησεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ τῆς παρακοῆς κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ εἰσβαλών· μάλιστα γὰρ ὁ κρατῶν θάνατος πρὸ τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημίας ἐβασίλευσε, κατὰ πάντων νόμον καὶ σκῆπτρον τῆς ἑαυτοῦ βασιλείας ἔχων τὴν παρακοήν. ἀλλ' οὐκ ἄναρχος ἢ ἀγέννητος ἡ τοῦ θανάτου βασιλεία· ἐκ γὰρ τῶν ζώντων τὸ τεθνάναι συμβαίνει, καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπηκόων ὑπακοῆς τὸ παρακοῦσαί τινα. τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὔ· ὃ γὰρ θέλω ἀγαθὸν τοῦτο οὐ ποιῶ, ἀλλ' ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο πράσσω. εἰ τὸ θέλειν μόνον ἐν ἡμῖν ἔστιν, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ θεληθὲν καλὸν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἡμῖν, εἰς μάτην ὁ ἀγαθὸς θεὸς τὰς ὁμοουσίας ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὰς ἐν τοῖς σώμασι κατέπεμψεν· τὸ γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ αὐταῖς φίλον οὐ πράττουσιν, οὐκ ἐνεργοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ μόνον θέλουσιν· τάχα δὲ οὐδ' αὐτό, ἄδηλον γάρ.
thought_title: The commandment is holy; sin became sinful beyond measure
orientation: Didymus is explaining Paul's words in Romans 7, arguing that the commandment and law are holy, just, and good, and that 'sin' means the devil, who became sinful beyond measure through the commandment.
pass_a_gloss: But so that some might not blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he used a neighboring and kindred word, saying such things: 'But we know that the law is holy and the commandment is holy and just and good.' Since therefore not even sin itself, that is the devil, is sin by nature and substance, he adds, saying: 'so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment.' For that which is something by substance will not admit the more and the less; for it is what it is, always being this which it is substantially. For that which comes to be and that which comes upon something, whether little or beyond measure, is other by substance than the things that come upon it; for quantity is not substance but is around the substance, not being substance. Therefore then the thing called sin by the apostle, admitting the more, will sin, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure. Therefore also of being sin, in which respect it is sin, it took a beginning, sin not being in the beginning sinful beyond measure according to having sinned. Wherefore indeed also he signifies the intensification of becoming sinful beyond measure in time to come, saying thus: 'so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment.' But if they should say: 'And how would the commandment and the law be good and just? And how holy, when through their occasion sin became sinful beyond measure, a sinner?' To these things let them hear that not, if something is harmed, is already also the occasion through which it is harmed base and evil; for not because those who gaze at the sun without pain and without measure are harmed in their eyes, do we already say that the sun is evil; nor because the devil has become sinful beyond measure by having plotted against the Son of God, do we already say that the Son of God is base and evil. 'But I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.' Now he explains into the person of Adam. And that having been deprived of having God in himself, having exchanged death for the truly real life—for not only the common death of his members mastered him, but also the death of disobedience entered against his soul; for especially the mastering death reigned before the coming of Christ, having disobedience as law and scepter of its own kingdom over all. But the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten; for dying happens from the living, and someone's disobeying from the obedience of the obedient. 'For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good is not; for the good that I will, this I do not do, but what I hate, this I practice.' If the willing alone is in us, but the working out of the willed good is not in us, in vain did the good God send down the souls of the same substance as himself into bodies; for they do not practice, they do not effect, what is dear to him and to them, but only will it; and perhaps not even this, for it is unclear.

choices.english: he used a neighboring and kindred word
choices.why: Didymus means Paul used a closely related expression (the law and commandment are holy) to forestall blame of God; 'neighboring and kindred' preserves the spatial and familial metaphor of the Greek.
The glossary requires 'sin' for ἁμαρτία and the phrase καθ' ὑπερβολήν means 'beyond measure' or 'exceedingly'; this rendering keeps the quantitative force Didymus is analyzing.

choices.term: τὸ πλέον καὶ τὸ ἔλαττον οὐκ ἐπιδέξεται
choices.english: will not admit the more and the less
choices.why: This is a technical philosophical phrase about substances not admitting degrees; the literal rendering preserves the Aristotelian flavor Didymus is invoking.
rejected: does not allow for more or less

choices.why: παράκειται literally means 'lies beside' or 'is at hand'; this preserves the spatial metaphor and the distinction Didymus draws between willing and working out.
rejected: the willing is present with me
to will is at hand for me

choices.english: souls of the same substance as himself
choices.why: ὁμοούσιος is a technical theological term; the literal rendering 'of the same substance' preserves its weight and the philosophical argument Didymus is making about the soul's nature.
ἀνόδως is unusual; it likely means 'without pain' or 'without harm' here, paired with ἀμέτρως 'without measure'; the literal rendering preserves the oddity of the Greek.

pass_b_english: But so that no one might blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he used a closely related and kindred word, saying: "We know that the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good" (Romans 7:12). Since not even sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance, he adds: "so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment" (Romans 7:13). For what is something by substance will not admit degrees of more and less; it is what it is, always being what it is essentially. But for what comes to be and has something added to it, whether little or beyond measure, it is other in substance than the things added to it. Quantity is not substance but is an attribute of substance, not being substance. Therefore the one called sin by the apostle admits the more of sinning, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure. So sin also received a beginning of being sin, insofar as it is sin, not being sinful beyond measure in the beginning according to its having sinned. Therefore he also signifies the intensification of becoming sinful beyond measure in time to come, saying: "so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment" (Romans 7:13). But if objectors should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just? How could they be holy, when through the opportunity they provided sin became sinful beyond measure? Let those who object hear in response that if something is harmed, the opportunity through which it is harmed is not therefore already base and evil. For it is not because those who gaze at the sun without method and without measure harm their eyes that we therefore call the sun evil. Nor is it because the devil became sinful beyond measure by having attacked the Son of God that we therefore say the Son of God is base and evil. "I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh" (Romans 7:18). Now Paul explains this as spoken in the person of Adam. And because he was deprived of having God in himself, he exchanged death instead of true life—for not only the common death of his members took hold of him, but also the death of disobedience entered against his soul. For the ruling death reigned especially before the coming of Christ, having disobedience as the law and scepter of its kingdom over all. But the kingdom of death is not without a ruler or unbegotten; for dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey. "For the will is present with me, but the working out of the good is not. For the good I will, this I do not do; but what I hate, this I practice" (Romans 7:18-19). If only the willing is in us, and the accomplishment of the willed good is not in us, then then one might say the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain. For they do not do what is dear to him and to them; they do not enact it, but only will it—and perhaps not even that, for even the willing is unclear.
notes: The source text has 'καθ' ὑπερ 4 βολὴν' with a line break and numeral 4, likely a page or column number inserted in the manuscript; the reading is καθ' ὑπερβολὴν.
The source text has 'αὐτῶν 2 ἁμαρτωλὸς' with a numeral 2, likely a page or column number; the reading is αὐτῶν ἁμαρτωλὸς.

problems.quote: without pain and without measure
problems.why: ἀνόδως means 'unmethodically, irrationally' or 'without system', not 'without pain'. The sun-gazing example is about improper method, not painlessness.
problems.fix: without method and without measure

problems.quote: having plotted against
problems.source_quote: τῷ ἐπικεχειρηκέναι κατὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ
problems.why: ἐπικεχειρηκέναι means 'to have attacked, made an attempt upon, set hands upon'—'having plotted against' weakens the sense of actual attack/assault. The devil's attack on Christ (temptation, crucifixion) is more than plotting.
problems.fix: by having attacked the Son of God
problems.ruling: ἐπικεχειρηκέναι is 'to attack/set hands on', not merely 'plotting'

problems.quote: Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is not sin by nature or substance, he adds:
problems.source_quote: Ἐπεὶ οὖν οὐδ' αὐτὴ ἡ ἁμαρτία, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ὁ διάβολος, φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ ἁμαρτία ἐστίν,
problems.why: Source says the devil (sin) *is* sin by nature and substance; English inserts a negation, flipping the meaning.
problems.fix: Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance, he adds:
problems.ruling: οὐδ' αὐτὴ ἁμαρτία...ἁμαρτία ἐστίν = 'not even sin itself...is sin'; English 'not' inverts to 'is not sin', contradicting Greek affirmation.

edits.old: without pain and without measure
edits.new: without method and without measure

edits.old: by having plotted against the Son of God
edits.new: by having attacked the Son of God

edits.old: Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is not sin by nature or substance, he adds:
edits.new: Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance, he adds:

fixed: ἀνόδως means 'without method' or 'irrationally', not 'without pain'; corrected to 'without method and without measure'.
ἐπικεχειρηκέναι means 'to have attacked' or 'made an attempt upon', not merely 'plotted against'; corrected to 'by having attacked the Son of God'.
Source reads 'οὐδ' αὐτὴ ἡ ἁμαρτία... φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ ἁμαρτία ἐστίν' — the devil *is* sin by nature and substance; the English negation was wrong and has been removed.

problems.quote: Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance
problems.source_quote: Ἐπεὶ οὖν οὐδ' αὐτὴ ἡ ἁμαρτία, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ὁ διάβολος, φύσει καὶ οὐσίᾳ ἁμαρτία ἐστίν
problems.why: Source has 'not even sin itself... is sin by nature' with οὐδ' and οὐκ; English drops both negatives, flipping meaning.
problems.fix: Since not even sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance
problems.ruling: Greek has οὐδ' … ἁμαρτία … ἔστιν (not even sin itself … is sin), English drops οὐδ' changing meaning.

problems.quote: he exchanged death for true life
problems.source_quote: ἀντὶ τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς θάνατον καταλλαξάμενος
problems.why: Greek means 'having exchanged death instead of true life,' i.e., got death in place of life; English reverses the exchange.
problems.fix: having exchanged death for true life
problems.ruling: Greek ἀντὶ τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς θάνατον καταλλαξάμενος = ‘exchanged death instead of true life’, English reverses direction.

problems.quote: the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten
problems.source_quote: ἀλλ' οὐκ ἄναρχος ἢ ἀγέννητος ἡ τοῦ θανάτου βασιλεία
problems.why: ἄναρχος means ‘without a ruler’, not ‘without beginning’; the translation changes the meaning.
problems.fix: the kingdom of death is not without a ruler nor unbegotten
problems.ruling: ἄναρχος = 'without beginning/ruler'; context demands 'without beginning' (contrasted with 'received a beginning' earlier), but 'without a ruler' is also valid. However, 'unbegotten' for ἀγέννητος confirms temporal/beginning sense is intended. Translation is correct, not error.

edits.old: Since sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance, he adds:
edits.new: Since not even sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance, he adds:

edits.old: he exchanged death for true life
edits.new: he exchanged death instead of true life

edits.old: the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten
edits.new: the kingdom of death is not without a ruler or unbegotten

fixed: Negation restored: source has οὐδ'...οὐκ, so 'not even sin itself...is sin by nature and substance' is correct.
Exchange direction corrected: source ἀντὶ τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς θάνατον καταλλαξάμενος means he got death in place of true life, so 'exchanged death instead of true life'.
ἄναρχος here means 'without a ruler', not 'without beginning'; corrected to 'without a ruler or unbegotten'.

problems.quote: But so that no one might blame the commandment or the God who gave it, Paul used a neighboring and kindred word, saying:
problems.source_quote: ἵνα δὲ μὴ τὴν ἐντολὴν ἢ τὸν ταύτην δεδωκότα θεὸν αἰτιάσωνταί τινες, γείτονι καὶ ὁμοσπόρῳ ἐχρήσατο ῥήματι τοιάδε φάσκων
problems.why: The Greek says “some (τινες) … used a neighboring word,” not Paul; agency is wrongly shifted to Paul.
problems.fix: But so that no one might blame the commandment or the God who gave it, some (people) used a neighboring and kindred word, saying:
problems.ruling: τινες is subject of αἰτιάσωνται, not ἐχρήσατο; Paul is ungrammatical insertion.

edits.old: But so that no one might blame the commandment or the God who gave it, Paul used a neighboring and kindred word, saying:
edits.new: But so that no one might blame the commandment or the God who gave it, some used a neighboring and kindred word, saying:

fixed: Agency: the Greek τινες is the subject of ἐχρήσατο, not Paul; the English wrongly inserted Paul as the agent. Changed to 'some used'.

problems.quote: But if they should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just?
problems.why: Unclear if this is Didymus imagining opponents, or quoting actual objectors, or a rhetorical device.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Didymus here imagines an objector.'

problems.quote: If only the willing is in us, and the working out of the willed good is not in us, then the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain.
problems.why: Sudden shift to first-person plural without clear speaker; seems to be Didymus arguing against an implied opponent, but could be misread as Paul's words.
problems.fix: Mark as Didymus's refutation of deterministic reading.

problems.quote: For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not
problems.why: Romans 7:18 is misquoted; 'lies beside me' is not standard English idiom for willingness.
problems.fix: Use standard rendering: 'to will is present with me, but to do the good is not.'

problems.quote: For what is something by substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is essentially. But for what comes to be and has something come upon it, whether little or beyond measure, it is other in substance than the things that come upon it. Quantity is not substance but is around substance, not being substance.
problems.why: Dense philosophical jargon barely coherent; 'other in substance than the things that come upon it' is opaque.
problems.fix: Simplify: 'What exists by nature cannot vary in degree; what acquires qualities can.'

problems.quote: the working out of the willed good
problems.why: 'Working out' as noun for 'accomplishment/performance' is awkward; Greek katergazesthai needs better rendering.
problems.fix: Use 'performance' or 'accomplishment' of the good.

problems.quote: the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not
problems.why: 'Willing lies beside me' is opaque; reader cannot parse the meaning.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'the desire is present in me, but the carrying-out of the good is not'

problems.quote: the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain
problems.why: Sudden introduction of a pre-existence/same-substance doctrine with no context; reads like an opponent's view.
problems.fix: Signal this is the impious view: 'then, as the impious say, the good God sent souls...'

problems.quote: dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey
problems.why: The second clause seems to say disobedience comes from obedience, which is self-contradictory.
problems.fix: Likely needs 'comes about alongside the obedience' or similar; check Greek.

problems.quote: the working-out precedes the work—as, for example, of a house or a ship
problems.why: 'Working-out' as technical term for preparation of material is never clearly defined for the reader.
problems.fix: Add brief gloss: 'the working-out (preparation of material) precedes the completed work'

problems.quote: But if they should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just?
problems.why: Unclear who 'they' are; reader cannot tell if this is an imagined objector or a named group.
problems.fix: Specify: 'But if opponents should say...' or 'But if someone should object...'

edits.old: For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not.
edits.new: For the willing is present with me, but the working out of the good is not.

edits.old: the working out of the willed good is not in us
edits.new: the accomplishment of the willed good is not in us

edits.old: dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey
edits.new: dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey

fixed: Speaker problem: 'But if they should say' — the source has 'εἰ δὲ λέγοιεν' (if they should say), which is a hypothetical objection Didymus raises; the English already conveys this with 'if they should say.' No edit needed.

Speaker problem: 'If only the willing is in us...' — the source has 'εἰ τὸ θέλειν μόνον ἐν ἡμῖν ἔστιν...' which is Didymus's own conditional argument, not a shift to Paul's voice. The English is clear enough; no edit needed.

Unreadable: 'For the willing lies beside me' — the source has 'τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι' (the willing lies beside me). 'Lies beside me' is a literal rendering of παράκειταί, but it is opaque in English. Changed to 'is present with me' to match standard English idiom for willingness.

Unreadable: 'For what is something by substance...' — the source is dense philosophical Greek; the English is a faithful rendering. The suggested simplification would lose the technical distinction Didymus is making. No edit needed.

Mistranslation: 'the working out of the willed good' — the source has 'τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ θεληθὲν καλὸν' (the working out of the willed good). 'Working out' is the glossary term for κατεργάζεσθαι, but as a noun it is awkward. Changed to 'accomplishment' for clarity while keeping the glossary verb elsewhere.
Unreadable: 'the willing lies beside me' — same as above; fixed.

Unreadable: 'the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain' — the source has 'εἰς μάτην ὁ ἀγαθὸς θεὸς τὰς ὁμοουσίας ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὰς ἐν τοῖς σώμασι κατέπεμψεν' (in vain did the good God send down the souls of the same substance as himself into bodies). This is Didymus's own statement, not an opponent's view. No edit needed.

Unreadable: 'dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey' — the source has 'ἐκ γὰρ τῶν ζώντων τὸ τεθνάναι συμβαίνει, καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπηκόων ὑπακοῆς τὸ παρακοῦσαί τινα' (for dying happens from the living, and someone's disobeying from the obedience of the obedient). The English 'comes from' is ambiguous; changed to 'comes about from' to clarify that disobedience arises from the context of obedience, not from obedience itself.
Unreadable: 'the working-out precedes the work...' — this text does not appear in the source or English; it is a false report. No edit needed.
Speaker problem: 'But if they should say' — same as first; no edit needed.

problems.quote: But if they should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just?
problems.why: Unclear if this is Didymus, a hypothetical objector, or the devil speaking.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'But if objectors should say...'

problems.quote: Now he explains this into the person of Adam.
problems.why: Non-idiomatic English; 'explains into' is not comprehensible.
problems.fix: Change to 'Now he applies this to the person of Adam.'

problems.quote: For the willing is present with me, but the working out of the good is not.
problems.why: Awkward calque from Greek; 'willing' as noun is obscure.
problems.fix: Use 'will' or 'willingness': 'For the will is present with me...'

problems.quote: For they do not do what is dear to him and to them; they do not enact it, but only will it—and perhaps not even that, for it is unclear.
problems.why: The argument is convoluted and the final clause 'for it is unclear' has no clear referent.
problems.fix: Clarify the logical structure and what is 'unclear.'

problems.quote: Quantity is not substance but is around substance, not being substance.
problems.why: Philosophical jargon mistranslated; 'around' for Greek 'peri' is opaque.
problems.fix: Use 'accident' or 'attribute': 'Quantity is not substance but an attribute of substance.'

problems.quote: Let them hear in response that if something is harmed
problems.why: Unclear who 'them' is; refers to hypothetical objectors but the antecedent is buried.
problems.fix: Specify: 'Let those who object hear…'

problems.quote: Now he explains this into the person of Adam.
problems.why: 'He' shifts referent from the devil to Paul without warning; reader may lose track.
problems.fix: Specify: 'Now Paul explains this as spoken in the person of Adam.'

variants.text: Now he explains this into the person of Adam.

problems.quote: for dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey.
problems.why: The second clause is nearly nonsensical: disobedience comes from obedience?
problems.fix: Likely means death spreads through one's disobedience, countered by others' obedience.

variants.text: for dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey.

problems.quote: the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain.
problems.why: Reads like a statement Didymus endorses, but it is an objection he rejects; grammar obscures this.
problems.fix: Mark as a hypothetical objection: 'If only the willing is in us… then one might say the good God sent souls…'

variants.text: the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain.

problems.quote: he used a neighboring and kindred word
problems.why: Odd phrasing; likely means a closely related or similar-sounding word, not 'neighboring.'
problems.fix: Use 'a closely related word' or 'a kindred expression.'

problems.quote: Quantity is not substance but is around substance, not being substance.
problems.why: 'Around substance' is a literal gloss of a philosophical term; not intelligible English.
problems.fix: Use 'surrounds substance' or 'is an attribute of substance, not substance itself.'

problems.quote: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18)
problems.why: Rom 7:18 reads 'in my flesh' not 'in me, that is, in my flesh'; the 'that is' is added.
problems.fix: Quote as: 'I know that good does not dwell in my flesh.'

variants.text: I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh

problems.quote: “For the willing is present with me, but the working out of the good is not. For the good I will, this I do not do; but what I hate, this I practice” (Romans 7:18-19)
problems.why: Rom 7:18 says 'the doing of the good is not'; 'working out' is non-standard for this verse.
problems.fix: Use 'the doing of the good is not' or note the rendering choice.

variants.text: the working out of the good is not

fixed: Speaker: 'But if they should say' — source has 'εἰ δὲ λέγοιεν' (if they should say), referring to hypothetical objectors; clarified as 'objectors'.
Unreadable: 'Now he explains this into the person of Adam' — source 'νῦν εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον ἐξηγεῖται' (now he explains into the person of Adam); 'he' is Paul, so specified.
Unreadable: 'For the willing is present with me' — source 'τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι' (for the willing lies beside me); 'willing' as noun is awkward; changed to 'will'.
Unreadable: 'for it is unclear' — source 'ἄδηλον γάρ' (for it is unclear); clarified referent as 'even the willing is unclear'.

Mistranslation: 'Quantity is not substance but is around substance' — source 'τὸ γὰρ πόσον οὐκ οὐσία ἀλλὰ περὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἐστίν' (quantity is not substance but is around substance); 'around' is literal; changed to 'attribute'.
Speaker: 'Let them hear in response' — source 'πρὸς ταῦτα ἀκουέτωσαν' (to these things let them hear); 'them' refers to objectors; clarified.

Unreadable: 'for dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey' — source 'ἐκ γὰρ τῶν ζώντων τὸ τεθνάναι συμβαίνει, καὶ ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὑπηκόων ὑπακοῆς τὸ παρακοῦσαί τινα' (for dying happens from the living, and someone's disobeying from the obedience of the obedient); English is accurate; no change.

Unreadable: 'the good God sent souls...' — source 'εἰς μάτην ὁ ἀγαθὸς θεὸς τὰς ὁμοουσίας ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὰς ἐν τοῖς σώμασι κατέπεμψεν' (in vain did the good God send down the souls...); this is part of a hypothetical objection; marked as such.

Mistranslation: 'he used a neighboring and kindred word' — source 'γείτονι καὶ ὁμοσπόρῳ ἐχρήσατο ῥήματι' (he used a neighboring and kindred word); 'neighboring' is literal; changed to 'closely related'.

Wrong scripture: 'I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh' — source quotes 'οἶδα δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἐμοί, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου, ἀγαθόν' (I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh); the 'that is' is in the source; no change.

Wrong scripture: 'For the willing is present with me...' — source quotes 'τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὔ' (for the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good is not); 'working out' is the glossary term for κατεργάζεσθαι; no change.

fixed.quote: some used a neighboring and kindred word, saying
fixed.fix: he used a neighboring and kindred word, saying
fixed.note: The verb ἐχρήσατο and the participle φάσκων are both singular and refer to Paul, not to an unnamed 'some'.

polish.changed: Clarified the philosophical language about substance and quantity, made the hypothetical objectors' question clearly attributed, smoothed the rendering of Romans 7:18, and clarified the shift to Didymus's own argument about souls and willing.

notes.why: Technical philosophical terms from Aristotelian/Neoplatonic metaphysics unexplained.
notes.fix: Gloss: 'more and less' = degrees of intensity vs. essential properties.

notes.quote: But if they should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just?
notes.why: Unclear if this is Didymus imagining opponents, or quoting actual objectors, or a rhetorical device.

notes.quote: If only the willing is in us, and the working out of the willed good is not in us, then the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain.
notes.why: Sudden shift to first-person plural without clear speaker; seems to be Didymus arguing against an implied opponent, but could be misread as Paul's words.
notes.fix: Mark as Didymus's refutation of deterministic reading.

notes.quote: For the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not
notes.why: Romans 7:18 is misquoted; 'lies beside me' is not standard English idiom for willingness.
notes.fix: Use standard rendering: 'to will is present with me, but to do the good is not.'

notes.quote: For what is something by substance will not admit the more and the less; it is what it is, always being what it is essentially. But for what comes to be and has something come upon it, whether little or beyond measure, it is other in substance than the things that come upon it. Quantity is not substance but is around substance, not being substance.
notes.why: Dense philosophical jargon barely coherent; 'other in substance than the things that come upon it' is opaque.
notes.fix: Simplify: 'What exists by nature cannot vary in degree; what acquires qualities can.'

notes.quote: the working out of the willed good
notes.why: 'Working out' as noun for 'accomplishment/performance' is awkward; Greek katergazesthai needs better rendering.

notes.quote: the willing lies beside me, but the working out of the good does not
notes.why: 'Willing lies beside me' is opaque; reader cannot parse the meaning.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'the desire is present in me, but the carrying-out of the good is not'

notes.quote: the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain
notes.why: Sudden introduction of a pre-existence/same-substance doctrine with no context; reads like an opponent's view.
notes.fix: Signal this is the impious view: 'then, as the impious say, the good God sent souls...'

notes.quote: dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes from the obedience of those who obey
notes.why: The second clause seems to say disobedience comes from obedience, which is self-contradictory.
notes.fix: Likely needs 'comes about alongside the obedience' or similar; check Greek.

notes.quote: the working-out precedes the work—as, for example, of a house or a ship
notes.why: 'Working-out' as technical term for preparation of material is never clearly defined for the reader.
notes.fix: Add brief gloss: 'the working-out (preparation of material) precedes the completed work'

notes.quote: the ruling death reigned especially before the coming of Christ
notes.why: 'Ruling death' as a personified force is introduced without explanation.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'death personified as a ruler' or 'the tyranny of death.'

notes.quote: the death of disobedience entered against his soul
notes.why: 'Death of disobedience' is a technical concept not explained; contrasted with 'common death of his members.'
notes.fix: Gloss: 'the spiritual death caused by disobedience'
